primary_sources: Angelina Grimké, Appeal to the Christian Women of the South, 1836

stimulus.text:
Angelina Grimké, Appeal to the Christian Women of the South (1836):

“But perhaps you will be ready to query, why appeal to women on this subject? We do not make the laws which perpetuate slavery. No legislative power is vested in us; we can do nothing to overthrow the system, even if we wished to do so. To this I reply, I know you do not make the laws, but I also know that you are the wives and mothers, the sisters and daughters of those who do; and if you really suppose you can do nothing to overthrow slavery, you are greatly mistaken. You can do much in every way: four things I will name. 1st. You can read on this subject. 2d. You can pray over this subject. 3d. You can speak on this subject. 4th. You can act on this subject.”

Grimké added that laws forbidding Southerners to free enslaved people or teach them to read, “such wicked laws ought to be no barrier in the way of your duty.”

Background: Grimké was born into a slaveholding family in Charleston, South Carolina, and had moved north to join the abolitionist cause.
stimulus.source_note: Quotations verbatim from Angelina Grimké, Appeal to the Christian Women of the South, The Anti-Slavery Examiner, September 1836, public domain, as printed on Wikisource.

source: original; stimulus verbatim from Angelina Grimké, Appeal to the Christian Women of the South (1836), public domain
stem: Grimké told Southern women they could 'act on this subject,' and that laws protecting slavery 'ought to be no barrier in the way of your duty.' Why did that message alarm Southern leaders?

options.text: She was asking Northern women to move to the South
options.misconception: Grimké addresses Southern women where they already live.

options.text: She was defending slavery as a positive good
options.misconception: Grimké calls slavery a sin and urges action against it.

options.text: She was asking Congress to raise the tariff
options.misconception: The passage says nothing about tariffs.

options.text: She was telling Southern women to disobey laws that protected slavery

rationales.A: Her readers are Southern women already. She does not ask anyone to move.
rationales.B: The whole appeal attacks slavery. A defense of slavery as a positive good is the opposite of her argument.
rationales.C: Tariffs never appear in the passage. Grimké writes about slavery and duty, not trade.
rationales.D: She tells readers that wicked laws should not stop them from acting. That is a call to disobey the laws that guard slavery.
rationales.general:
1. Read the boldest line. Grimké says laws protecting slavery ought to be no barrier to duty.
2. Ask who hears that line. Southern leaders enforced those laws and banned abolitionist writing.
3. Name the alarm. A call to disobey, sent to Southern women, struck at the laws themselves.
Background: Southern states banned the circulation of abolitionist pamphlets in the 1830s.
Remember: a message alarms rulers when it tells ordinary people to disobey.
